title: What artificial intelligence cannot write
body: In a little over a decade we've gone from systems that could recognize cats in photos to models capable of writing code, reasoning through complex problems, and holding a conversation that, for several minutes, is indistinguishable from a person's. The leap hasn't been gradual: it's been a series of leaps, each one faster than the last. And with each leap, the question has shifted from "can it do this?" to "how far should it go?".

That's where the real controversy lies, and it isn't technical. Some argue that slowing development down would be a historic mistake: that a technology capable of accelerating medical research, democratizing access to knowledge, or solving problems we've been stuck on for decades deserves to move as fast as it possibly can, with no brake beyond our own ability to build it. Others see that very speed as the problem: a race between a handful of companies and countries, with enormous financial incentives and very little oversight, deciding on behalf of the rest of humanity what role is left for us.

I don't have a clean answer to that debate, and I suspect no one does yet. But I do have one conviction, and it's the one I want to share here: whatever the technology ends up doing, there is a territory that will remain ours, and today it's worth remembering that.

A model can write a poem with perfect meter. It can imitate any painter's style, compose a melody that sounds like Bach or Bowie, generate a thousand variations of a script in seconds. What it cannot do is have lived what it writes. Behind a good poem there's a real loss, a night you never forget, a decision that cost something. Art isn't valuable for the technical skill with which it's executed — a machine, I'll admit, keeps getting better at that — but for the human experience holding it up. That part can't be automated, because it isn't a computational problem. It's simply having lived.

That's why I believe the answer to automation isn't to compete on the ground where we're going to lose, but to invest in the ground where no competition is possible. The cheaper it becomes to generate content, the more valuable everything carrying a real voice, a genuine point of view, a lived life, will become. The humanities, art, philosophy, culture, are not the luxury we get to afford once technology does the hard work: they are, increasingly, the part of the work no technology can do for us.

I work with code every day, and I feel no luddite nostalgia toward these tools: I use them, they help me, and I genuinely believe they'll keep changing how we work. But that's exactly why I insist on this: automating the technical doesn't free us from being human, it demands we be better at it. If AI takes repetitive work off our hands, let that free up time for what truly cannot be replicated. The rest, let whoever wants to write it. I'd rather keep writing what only I could have lived.
